info.bio: Grateful Dead (también conocidos entre sus seguidores como "The Dead") fue un grupo de rock americano influenciado por la psicodelia. Creado en 1965 por integrantes de otro grupo, "Mother McCree's Uptown Jug Champions", Grateful Dead se dieron a conocer gracias a su estilo de composición único y ecléctico --que fusionaba elementos del rock, folk, bluegrass, blues, country y jazz-- y por las largas improvisaciones que realizaban en sus actuaciones.

scenes.name: San Francisco: Acid Tests y Haight-Ashbury
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: A principios de 1966 había distritos psicodélicos con locales, grupos, ropa, impresos y drogas propios en Londres, Los Ángeles y San Francisco. Los Merry Pranksters de Ken Kesey convirtieron su desafío «Can You Pass the Acid Test?» en fiestas de luces, cine y sonido grabado y devuelto al instante: la segunda, en San José en diciembre de 1965 tras un concierto de los Stones, y nueve más en los tres primeros meses de 1966 (cinco en Los Ángeles, una en Watts). Los beats se habían mudado de North Beach a Haight-Ashbury; los Thelin abrieron la Psychedelic Shop y con Stewart Brand se hizo el Trips Festival (6.000 personas). La banda sonora era Rubber Soul. El caos sustituía al cuidado de Leary por el «set and setting»: en el Acid Test de Watts, Ken Babbs amplificó por micrófono los gritos de una chica en pleno mal viaje.

scenes.name: Los Diggers y la comida gratis
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Salidos de la San Francisco Mime Troupe y del Artists Liberation Front e inspirados por los Provos, Emmett Grogan, Billy Murcott, Peter Berg y otros tomaron el nombre de los radicales ingleses de Gerrard Winstanley (1649) y publicaron hojas anónimas contra la sociedad americana, contra los comerciantes hip de Haight Street y contra el «trascendentalismo psicodélico» de Leary. Durante el toque de queda de Hunters Point animaron a desafiarlo sin enfrentarse. Hacia el 6 de octubre, el día en que el LSD se hizo ilegal en California (celebrado con el Love Pageant Rally en el Panhandle, con los Grateful Dead y Big Brother), empezaron a dar comida gratis cada día a los jóvenes y fugados que llegaban al Haight: «es gratis porque es tuyo». El Haight ya tenía periódicos, salas, grafismo y sonido propios; Newsweek pensó que podía arrasar el país.

scenes.name: Psicodelia y acid-rock
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: En 1965 San Francisco se convierte en la ciudad más efervescente del país: los Grateful Dead tocan en los «acid tests» de Ken Kesey, nace la escena hippy y en 1966-67 llega el verano del amor. El acid-rock, evolución del folk-rock pensada como banda sonora del viaje de LSD, es el equivalente rockero de la pintura abstracta, el free jazz y la poesía beat: su gran invento es la «jam», con la guitarra eléctrica al mando y un espíritu zen en lugar del dolor del blues. Jefferson Airplane encarnan la era; los Grateful Dead inventan la improvisación colectiva libre (Anthem Of The Sun, Live Dead); Kaleidoscope, Moby Grape, Quicksilver, Blue Cheer o Fifty Foot Hose amplían el abanico. Monterey y Sgt Pepper (1967) convierten lo alternativo en mainstream. Fuera de California, Jimi Hendrix declara la guerra a la armonía occidental con su guitarra.

scenes.name: Sonidos progresivos de los noventa
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Phish devuelven el rock alternativo a la radio y legitiman el regreso a la estética progresiva, sobre todo en la Costa Este: Blues Traveler, Motherhead Bug y Sulfur, Spin Doctors, Klezmatics, Cul De Sac (Ecim, China Gate) y Run On. El noise-punk-jazz de God Is My Co-pilot, Molecules, Love Child, Blowhole, Harry Pussy. Virginia como epicentro (Echolyn, Boud Deun, Rake, Dave Matthews Band). Solistas: Marc Ribot, Nicky Skopelitis, Buckethead, Loren Mazzacane, los zappianos Ant-Bee y Mike Keneally, Gary Lucas, Alan Licht, Bob Drake. En la Costa Oeste, Primus (Frizzle Fry), Mr Bungle, Amy Denio, Caveman Shoestore, Thessalonians. Internacional: Philharmonie, Xaal, Volapuk, Kevin Martin (God, Techno Animal, Ice, Bug). Y la Babel final: Bright, Meringue, Cerberus Shoal, Tin Hat Trio, Species Being.

scenes.name: La segunda venida del industrial
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: En los noventa el estilo brutal de Nine Inch Nails lo invade todo en EE UU y el industrial se vuelve fenómeno de masas; el «aggro» de KMFDM es menos visible pero igual de ubicuo: Grotus, Filter, Stabbing Westward, Acumen, Skrew, Electric Hellfire Club, Society Burning, Gravity Kills y, lo más original, Girls Vs Boys (Venus Luxure No.1 Baby) y New Wet Kojak. La EBM internacional se vuelve más brutal (Leaether Strip, Suicide Commando, :Wumpscut:, Hocico, Mentallo & The Fixer). La «música de la fábrica de la muerte» sobrevive en los escultores de ruido: los neozelandeses Dead C (Harsh '70s Reality, «música imposible de escuchar»), Gate, Bruce Russell, Namanax, Illusion Of Safety, Maeror Tri, Towering Inferno (Kaddish). Y el «digital hardcore» de Atari Teenage Riot y Alec Empire.

podcast.title: Formation and Early Influence (1965)
podcast.body: The Grateful Dead formed in 1965 in the Bay Area and were a focal point of the 1960s psychedelic scene. "The Grateful Dead formed in 1965 in the Bay Area and they were obviously a focal point of the 60s psychedelic scene."

podcast.title: First Modern Concert T-Shirt (1966)
podcast.body: The Grateful Dead pioneered the modern concert T-shirt with a design featuring their iconic skeleton-in-roses logo, created by Stanley Mouse in 1966. This marked a significant shift in perception, as selling merch was previously considered "uncool" and "too commercial." "And this has gone down in history as the first modern concert T-shirt, a grateful dead shirt."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Development of the Wall of Sound (1972-1973)
podcast.body: Following the realization that their existing system was inadequate, The Grateful Dead's crew embarked on a year-long experimentation with PA gear, led by Owsley "Bear" Stanley. Their efforts culminated in the unveiling of the revolutionary "Wall of Sound" in 1973, a system designed to drastically improve live sound. "Over the next year, their crew experimented with PA gear, led by a former ballet dancer from Kentucky turned LSD drug dealer name Ausley Bear Stanley."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Sound System Inadequacy (1972)
podcast.body: In 1972, The Grateful Dead held a meeting in their Novato, California, warehouse practice space to discuss the inadequacy of their concert sound. Their system, designed by Bob Hyal in 1968, utilized Alltec's "Voice of the Theater" series cabinets, radial horns (a novel inclusion at the time), ring tweeters, and a custom crossover, and while "better than most," it was deemed "lacking by 1972" for the band's needs.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Wall of Sound (1972)
podcast.body: The Grateful Dead pioneered concert amplification with their "Wall of Sound" setup in 1972, which represented a significant breakthrough in modern concert sound. This system generated at least 26,000 watts, and possibly up to 30,000 watts, marking a massive leap in power and clarity for live music and establishing new standards for large-scale concert sound. "when it comes to modern day concert amplification, it was the grateful dead who really broke through with their wall of sound setup in 1972."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Wall of Sound (1973)
podcast.body: The "Wall of Sound" was an innovative and massive concert sound system unveiled by The Grateful Dead in 1973. It weighed 75 tons, stood three stories tall, was 100 feet wide, and required four semis and 21 people for transport. The system contained hundreds of speakers, specifically 568 JBLs and approximately 50 Electro Voice tweeters, powered by mostly Macintosh tube amps pumping out around 26,000 watts. Vocals went through one set of speakers while instrumentation went through others, arranged in "line arrays" for even sound dispersion. "The wall contained hundreds of speakers, 568 JBLs, and about 50 electro voice tweeters, to be specific, along with amplifiers, mostly Macintosh tube amps, pumping out something around 26,000 watts, which was absolutely insane for its day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Wall of Sound Debut and Dismantling (1974)
podcast.body: The Grateful Dead's "Wall of Sound" made its debut at the Cow Palace in San Francisco on March 23, 1974. Despite its impressive scale and sound quality—described as "so loud and so clear that it sounded great at a quarter of a mile"—it proved to be too expensive to operate and maintain. Consequently, the band had the system dismantled within a year of its introduction. "Within a year, though, it proved to be too expensive, and the band headed dismantled."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Grateful Dead Designated Taping Zones (1984) – First Major Band to Officially Allow Fan Recording
podcast.body: After years of tolerating the tape-trading community that had formed around their unique live shows, the Grateful Dead formally began allowing and even designating special taping zones at their concerts in 1984, setting a precedent for the acceptance of fan recordings. "In 1984, they began allowing and designating 'recording zones' for fans, setting a precedent."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Robert Hunter's Songwriting Recognition (1994)
podcast.body: Robert Hunter, who wrote almost all a significant portion of the Grateful Dead's songs but never played an instrument for them, was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame alongside the band in 1994, acknowledging his crucial role. "Robert Hunter wrote almost all a significant portion of the Grateful Dead songs. He did not play a note for the band, but his role as songwriter is so important that when the dead were inducted into the rock and roll hall of fame in 1994, he was inducted along with them."

podcast.title: Clash and Accommodation with Ticketmaster
podcast.body: The Grateful Dead engaged in a confrontation with Ticketmaster over the issue of service fees, similar to battles faced by other bands. Despite the challenges, they successfully held their ground and eventually negotiated an equitable agreement with Ticketmaster, maintaining control over their unique ticketing system. "They held their ground and eventually reached an equitable deal with ticket master."

podcast.body: The Grateful Dead offered a unique merchandise item in 2020: deodorant that reportedly smelled like "matured." "Grateful dead deodorant. And yes, it does smell like matured."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Direct-to-Fan Ticketing (1970s)
podcast.body: The Grateful Dead developed and maintained a highly efficient direct-to-fan mail order ticketing platform called Grateful Dead Ticket Service during the 1970s. This system allowed them to sell thousands of tickets directly to their dedicated fanbase, known as "deadheads," and gave them significant control over ticket distribution, which they were unwilling to relinquish. "Over years and years, the dead built up their own mail order ticketing platform called Grateful Dead Ticket Service."

podcast.title: Festival Express Experience
podcast.body: Bob Weir noted that there was little sleeping but much drinking on the Festival Express train, a new experience for the band members who typically used LSD and pot. The booze was also reportedly dosed with psychedelics, leading them to "achieve liftoff." They ran out of alcohol before reaching Winnipeg, prompting an unscheduled stop to clear out a liquor store. "Bob Weir of the Grateful Dead said that there was really not a whole lot of sleeping on this train but there was a lot of drinking which was something that he and his bandmates were as he put it new to."

podcast.body: The Grateful Dead's innovative approach to ticketing and their successful negotiation with Ticketmaster served as a model and source of advice for other prominent bands, including U2 and Pearl Jam, who later sought to challenge the established ticketing system. "Several bands took notice of what the dead did and asked them for advice."

podcast.title: Rarely Made Music Videos
podcast.body: The Grateful Dead rarely embraced the idea of making music videos, in contrast to the industry's push for them. Their reluctance highlighted the resistance from some artists against the burgeoning music video industry and its financial demands. "The grateful dead rarely touched the idea."

podcast.title: Shift to Folk Rock in the 1970s
podcast.body: As the 1970s approached, the Grateful Dead shifted from sprawling studio experiments and psychedelic rock to a folk rock approach, characterized by concise songwriting, storytelling, stripped-down arrangements, and a focus on Americana traditions like Appalachian, Bakersfield Country Sound, and Front Porch Folk storytelling. "But as the 70s approached, they were taking more of a folk rock approach. We don't have any more of these sprawling studio experiments. Instead we have very concise songwriting, we have storytelling, we have stripped down arrangements."

podcast.title: Wall of Sound Feedback
podcast.body: The Grateful Dead were known for their live performances, where "Deadheads" (fans) would experience extended periods of guitar screeches and feedback. These were amplified through the band's custom-designed "Wall of Sound" PA system, creating an immersive and powerful auditory experience. "Deadheads were often treated to long whales of guitar screeches, played through the band's custom wall of sound PA system."

xref.title: First Modern Concert T-Shirt (1966)
xref.body: The Grateful Dead pioneered the modern concert T-shirt with a design featuring their iconic skeleton-in-roses logo, created by Stanley Mouse in 1966. This marked a significant shift in perception, as selling merch was previously considered "uncool" and "too commercial." "And this has gone down in history as the first modern concert T-shirt, a grateful dead shirt."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Development of the Wall of Sound (1972-1973)
xref.body: Following the realization that their existing system was inadequate, The Grateful Dead's crew embarked on a year-long experimentation with PA gear, led by Owsley "Bear" Stanley. Their efforts culminated in the unveiling of the revolutionary "Wall of Sound" in 1973, a system designed to drastically improve live sound. "Over the next year, their crew experimented with PA gear, led by a former ballet dancer from Kentucky turned LSD drug dealer name Ausley Bear Stanley."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Sound System Inadequacy (1972)
xref.body: In 1972, The Grateful Dead held a meeting in their Novato, California, warehouse practice space to discuss the inadequacy of their concert sound. Their system, designed by Bob Hyal in 1968, utilized Alltec's "Voice of the Theater" series cabinets, radial horns (a novel inclusion at the time), ring tweeters, and a custom crossover, and while "better than most," it was deemed "lacking by 1972" for the band's needs.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Wall of Sound (1972)
xref.body: The Grateful Dead pioneered concert amplification with their "Wall of Sound" setup in 1972, which represented a significant breakthrough in modern concert sound. This system generated at least 26,000 watts, and possibly up to 30,000 watts, marking a massive leap in power and clarity for live music and establishing new standards for large-scale concert sound. "when it comes to modern day concert amplification, it was the grateful dead who really broke through with their wall of sound setup in 1972."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: The Wall of Sound (1973)
xref.body: The "Wall of Sound" was an innovative and massive concert sound system unveiled by The Grateful Dead in 1973. It weighed 75 tons, stood three stories tall, was 100 feet wide, and required four semis and 21 people for transport. The system contained hundreds of speakers, specifically 568 JBLs and approximately 50 Electro Voice tweeters, powered by mostly Macintosh tube amps pumping out around 26,000 watts. Vocals went through one set of speakers while instrumentation went through others, arranged in "line arrays" for even sound dispersion. "The wall contained hundreds of speakers, 568 JBLs, and about 50 electro voice tweeters, to be specific, along with amplifiers, mostly Macintosh tube amps, pumping out something around 26,000 watts, which was absolutely insane for its day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Wall of Sound Debut and Dismantling (1974)
xref.body: The Grateful Dead's "Wall of Sound" made its debut at the Cow Palace in San Francisco on March 23, 1974. Despite its impressive scale and sound quality—described as "so loud and so clear that it sounded great at a quarter of a mile"—it proved to be too expensive to operate and maintain. Consequently, the band had the system dismantled within a year of its introduction. "Within a year, though, it proved to be too expensive, and the band headed dismantled."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Grateful Dead Designated Taping Zones (1984) – First Major Band to Officially Allow Fan Recording
xref.body: After years of tolerating the tape-trading community that had formed around their unique live shows, the Grateful Dead formally began allowing and even designating special taping zones at their concerts in 1984, setting a precedent for the acceptance of fan recordings. "In 1984, they began allowing and designating 'recording zones' for fans, setting a precedent."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: All-Female San Francisco Group
xref.body: Ace of Cups was an all-female group formed in San Francisco in 1967, featuring Diane Metilige on drums. They were noted for opening for Jimi Hendrix and maintaining friendships with prominent bands like Jefferson Airplane and The Grateful Dead, marking their presence in the late 1960s psychedelic rock scene. "They were at all-female group formed in 1967 and featured die-end metallige on drums."

xref.title: Associated with Influential Bay Area Bands
xref.body: The band were friends with other prominent San Francisco bands of the era, including the Grateful Dead and the Jefferson Airplane, demonstrating their integration into the vibrant local music scene. xref.title: Clash and Accommodation with Ticketmaster
xref.body: The Grateful Dead engaged in a confrontation with Ticketmaster over the issue of service fees, similar to battles faced by other bands. Despite the challenges, they successfully held their ground and eventually negotiated an equitable agreement with Ticketmaster, maintaining control over their unique ticketing system. "They held their ground and eventually reached an equitable deal with ticket master."

xref.title: Deodorant with "Matured" Scent as Merchandise
xref.body: The Grateful Dead offered a unique merchandise item in 2020: deodorant that reportedly smelled like "matured." "Grateful dead deodorant. And yes, it does smell like matured."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Distinct Musical Identity
xref.body: The band gained attention in the early 1990s because their sound was distinct and set them apart. They were explicitly "not part of the whole grunge thing" and "certainly not very punk," instead offering a "fresh reinvention of some classic rock moves in the vein of the grateful dead and Leonard Skinnerd." "They were definitely not part of the whole grunge thing, and they were certainly not very punk. Their sound was a fresh reinvention of some classic rock moves in the vein of the grateful dead and Leonard Skinnerd, and it really made them stand out from the crowd."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Direct-to-Fan Ticketing (1970s)
xref.body: The Grateful Dead developed and maintained a highly efficient direct-to-fan mail order ticketing platform called Grateful Dead Ticket Service during the 1970s. This system allowed them to sell thousands of tickets directly to their dedicated fanbase, known as "deadheads," and gave them significant control over ticket distribution, which they were unwilling to relinquish. "Over years and years, the dead built up their own mail order ticketing platform called Grateful Dead Ticket Service."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Weird History of Concert Tickets Part 2

xref.title: Early Exposure to Drugs
xref.body: Courtney Love's struggles with substance abuse began early; her mother reportedly gave her Valium at age 8. Her biological father, associated with the Grateful Dead, also exposed her to drugs. She started with marijuana, then various opiates including heroin by 16, and cocaine by 19. "When she acted up, her mom apparently fed her volume at age 8."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Musical Influences
xref.body: While initially struggling to find music he liked despite a musical household, by age 15, Declan McManus became a fan of The Grateful Dead and The Band, a Canadian group known for backing Ronnie Hawkins and Bob Dylan. These influences shaped his early musical interests before he gravitated towards punk and new wave. "By the time he was 15, though, he had become something of a fan of the grateful dead. He also was a big fan of the band, that Canadian group that backed up both Ronnie Hawkins and Bob Dylan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.body: Sound City hosted a wide range of influential artists, including Metallica, Johnny Cash, REO Speedwagon, Nine Inch Nails, Grateful Dead, Weezer, Red Hot Chili Peppers, Tool, Blind Melon, Slipknot, and Queens of the Stone Age. xref.title: Formation and Early Connections
xref.body: Formed in San Francisco in 1967, coinciding with the Summer of Love, Ace of Cups consisted of five women without any male members. They were friends with The Grateful Dead and Jefferson Airplane, and Jimi Hendrix was so impressed that he invited them to open one of his gigs at Golden Gate Park. "They were formed in San Francisco in 1967, right in time for the summer of love."

xref.title: Large Bluegrass Ensemble
xref.body: Winston Marshall's Bluegrass group featured up to 16 members. They performed covers of artists ranging from The Grateful Dead, Neil Young, and Dexys Midnight Runners to Shania Twain, and played at a small 40-person bar in London called The Bosens Locker. "His sort of Bluegrass group was called Captain Kick and the Cowboy Ramblers, and it had up to 16 members."

xref.title: Pseudo-Stepdad's Record Collection
xref.body: His mother's boyfriend, Chip Donaldson, who was an English teacher and Vietnam veteran, moved in with his own record collection featuring music from the late 1960s and early 1970s, including artists like The Rolling Stones, Bob Dylan, and Grateful Dead. "It featured a lot of stuff from the late 60s and early 70s. Stones, Dylan, grateful dad, that kind of thing."
